facts.text: On this date in 1989, Hungary opened its border with Austria, allowing 15,000 East Germans to flee West — the single largest breach of the Iron Curtain before the Wall fell.
On this date in 1953, John F. Kennedy married Jacqueline Bouvier in Newport, Rhode Island, before a crowd of 700 guests and a mob of 3,000 uninvited onlookers outside.
More people live inside a 40-mile radius of Manila than in the entire country of Australia.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined — roughly 60% of the world's total freshwater lakes sit within its borders.
Tokyo's greater metropolitan area produces an economy larger than Canada's entire GDP, making it the most economically productive urban zone in human history.

On this date in 1992, the British pound collapsed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. George Soros made $1 billion in a single day. The UK Treasury lost £3.3 billion defending a peg it could not hold.
On this date in 1988, Lehman Brothers went public at $5 a share. Twenty years later, almost to the week, it filed the largest bankruptcy in American history with $613 billion in debt.
The S&P 500 has spent more time below its all-time high than above it. On average, it takes 1.9 years to recover a peak — but the average masks crashes that took over a decade.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway holds more cash than the GDP of Portugal. At its 2024 peak, the cash pile exceeded $277 billion — more than most nations produce in a year.
The Dutch East India Company, adjusted for inflation, was worth roughly $8 trillion at its peak — more than Apple, Microsoft, and Saudi Aramco combined today.
On this date in 1959, Luna 2 became the first human-made object to reach another world, crashing into the Moon at 3.3 km/s after a 36-hour flight from Earth.
On September 12, 1962, Kennedy declared the US would go to the Moon — at that moment, NASA had accumulated a total of 9 hours of human spaceflight experience.
Your skeleton is not a fixed structure. Every atom of calcium in your bones will be replaced within the next decade through a process called remodeling, running continuously right now.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.

The mantis shrimp sees the world through 16 types of photoreceptors — humans have 3 — yet research shows it processes color with less sophistication, using the extra channels as a rapid identification shortcut.
On this day in 1940, teenagers discovered the Lascaux cave paintings — art 17,000 years old, stumbled upon by four boys and a dog following a fallen tree.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. It is older than most things people call 'ancient'.
On this day in 1962, Kennedy promised to go to the Moon. The Apollo computers that got there had less processing power than a modern greeting card.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was as distant from the pyramids as we are from Julius Caesar.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — before the telephone, before the lightbulb, and 140 years before most offices actually started using one.

Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and gone. Linguists consider it untranslatable — English requires an entire sentence to approximate what Portuguese captures in four syllables.
Hiraeth (Welsh): homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or never had. The word holds grief and nostalgia simultaneously, a distinction Welsh makes that English simply cannot.

On this date in 1609, Henry Hudson sailed into the river that now bears his name. The Lenape people called it Muhheakantuck — 'the river that flows both ways' — capturing its tidal nature in a single word.
Petrichor: coined in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and R.G. Thomas, from Greek petra (stone) and ichor (the fluid in gods' veins). It names the scent of rain on dry earth.

On September 12, 1962, Kennedy declared the moon goal at Rice University. The speech used 'We choose' — a deliberate rhetorical anaphora the speechwriters borrowed from classical Latin oratory, called conduplicatio.
On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal, triggering a 30% Bitcoin crash within days — yet 90% of those price levels were recovered within six weeks.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting the network's energy consumption by roughly 99.95%.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named in Satoshi Nakamoto's whitepaper — the term was coined by forum users in 2010 and only later became canonical.
The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a flaw in Ethereum — it exploited a flaw in one contract written on top of it, a distinction the community largely ignored when deciding to hard fork.
Bitcoin's UTXO model means your wallet holds no coins — it holds cryptographic claims to unspent outputs, and your 'balance' is software arithmetic performed locally at query time.
On this date in 2012, AlexNet's training run that would win ImageNet by a 10.9-point margin over the runner-up was already underway — a gap so large the organizers assumed a scoring error.
Today in 2017, Google Brain published the Transformer paper. Every major language model since — GPT, BERT, Gemini, Claude — runs on that architecture unchanged in its essentials.
GPT-4 was trained on roughly 25,000 A100 GPUs running for 90–100 days. The electricity alone cost an estimated $63 million at US commercial rates.
Chinchilla scaling laws, published in 2022, showed that most large models of the era were undertrained by a factor of 4–10x — meaning companies had spent billions training models on too little data.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins before most structural biology labs had time to read the paper. The entire prior PDB database held roughly 180,000 experimentally solved structures.
